H1       open         c=0.75 The score is mainly set by how many epochs it takes to reach mean accuracy >=0.753. Changes that improve sample efficiency (architecture, optimizer, label smoothing, data selection, averaging) cut time far more than anything else, taking it from the 59.3 s ResNet9 baseline to roughly 10 s.

Settings: frozen patch-whitening, dirac init, BatchNorm-bias lr x64, lookahead, alternating flip, depth 3, widths 128/384/~576, label smoothing 0.3, lr 9, wd 0.012, batch size 1024. TTA is forbidden by RULES.md.
    H1.1.1   open         c=0.60 Without TTA, the airbench96-style recipe (128/384/576, depth 3, LS 0.3) at <=10 epochs reaches mean accuracy >=0.753 on seeds 0-2, with time <=12 s on the A100-SXM4. The baseline is 59.3 s.
    H1.1.2   open         c=0.55 The same recipe at the reported 8.5 epochs, without TTA, lands below 0.753 (expected 0.744-0.752). Getting back to >=0.753 takes >=1 extra epoch, consistent with TTA being worth about 0.65 pp or about 1.2 epochs.
    H1.1.3   open         c=0.50 Between 8 and 11 epochs, accuracy rises by >=0.4 pp per extra epoch and roughly linearly. So the knee at 0.753 can be found to within 0.5 epochs (about 5% of time) from a 3-4 point epoch sweep.
  H1.2     open         c=0.50 Using Muon (orthogonalized momentum) for the 4D conv filters and fused Nesterov SGD for biases and the head, at batch size about 2000, cuts the epochs and wall-clock time needed on CIFAR-100. This mirrors airbench94_muon on CIFAR-10.
    H1.2.1   open         c=0.40 Muon (lr ~0.24, momentum 0.6, nesterov) on the conv filters at batch size 2000 with linear decay to zero reaches >=0.753 in >=10% less time than the tuned SGD airbench96-style base at its own knee.
  H1.3     open         c=0.55 With 100 classes and short training, stronger label smoothing (about 0.3) regularizes better than the CIFAR-10 default of 0.2. This raises accuracy at a fixed epoch count.
    H1.3.1   open         c=0.45 At a fixed recipe and epoch count, LS 0.3 gives >=0.3 pp higher mean accuracy than LS 0.2. LS 0.4 is no better than 0.3 (within 0.15 pp or worse).

    H1.4.1   open         c=0.30 Training on the hardest 50% of each batch (selected by a small proxy model) reaches >=0.753 with >=10% less time than full-batch training at the matched-accuracy knee.
  H1.5     open         c=0.50 Widening the last block buys accuracy more cheaply than adding epochs. The final 576-channel block adds little compute, while CIFAR-100's 100-way head benefits from more capacity.
    H1.5.1   open         c=0.40 Widening the last block from 512 to 576 at a fixed epoch count gives >=0.3 pp accuracy for <=5% more time per epoch. Net effect: lower time at the 0.753 knee than the 512-wide version.
H2       open         c=0.60 With the recipe and epochs held fixed, per-step GPU efficiency is a major share of what remains of the time. That covers precision, memory format, kernel fusion and optimizer or Python launch overhead. Systems work can cut time by 10-30% with no change in accuracy.
  H2.1     open         c=0.70 torch.compile (max-autotune) with channels_last and fp16/bf16 autocast (BatchNorm in fp32) raises throughput substantially. Compilation and warmup happen in build() on synthetic data, so they are untimed.
    H2.1.1   open         c=0.60 A compiled, channels_last, half-precision training step cuts train time by >=20% against the same recipe run eagerly in fp32/TF32. Mean accuracy changes by no more than 0.2 pp.
  H2.2     open         c=0.50 Hiverge-style engineering cuts the remaining per-step overhead in a run of a few seconds: a vectorized or fused optimizer update (foreach/fused, or batched Muon), a fully compiled train step, and SiLU instead of GELU.
    H2.2.1   open         c=0.40 On top of H2.1, a fused/foreach optimizer plus a single compiled train step (forward, backward and update) reduces time by >=8%, with accuracy within 0.2 pp.
  H2.3     open         c=0.30 Progressive resizing, i.e. training the early epochs at lower resolution (cropping to about 24 px) and finishing at 32 px, lowers total FLOPs with little loss in final accuracy. Each resolution is compiled in build().
    H2.3.1   open         c=0.25 Running the first ~35% of epochs at 24 px and the rest at 32 px reaches >=0.753 with >=8% less time than training at 32 px throughout. The comparison is at the matched knee and may allow added epochs.
H3       open         c=0.50 Fixed overheads in the timed prepare/train are >10% of a run of about 10 s. These include loading and decoding data on 4 CPUs, host-to-device copies, normalization, whitening fit, CPU augmentation, and compile or autotune that leaks into the timed region. They can be cut without changing the learning recipe, while staying within the rules.
  H3.1     open         c=0.60 Keep the whole training set on the GPU as a uint8/half tensor, loaded in prepare, and run augmentation (flip, translate/crop, cutout) as vectorized GPU ops. This removes the bottleneck of a 4-CPU dataloader.
    H3.1.1   open         c=0.50 With data and augmentation on the GPU, prepare (load, transfer, normalize, whitening fit) takes <=1.0 s, and per-epoch time is not CPU-bound: GPU utilization stays >=90% during train.
  H3.2     open         c=0.60 Every compile, autotune and warmup happens in build() on synthetic inputs, covering every shape used later (full and final partial train batch, eval batch sizes). That way nothing recompiles inside the timed region, and no real data is touched in build.
    H3.2.1   open         c=0.60 After warmup in build, the first epoch's time is within 10% of later epochs, and no recompilation happens during prepare or train. Eval of any batch size B=1..1024 finishes in <5 s.

  H4.1     open         c=0.55 With seeds fixed, repeated runs of the same recipe differ only through nondeterministic kernels and GPU timing jitter. Both are small compared with the effects we want to detect.
    H4.1.1   open         c=0.60 Rerunning an identical recipe 2-3 times gives a spread in mean accuracy of <=0.15 pp and a spread in mean time of <=3%. Smaller differences are marked inconclusive (~).
  H4.2     open         c=0.50 Weight averaging (lookahead or EMA) raises accuracy at low epoch counts and lowers the spread across seeds. This allows fewer epochs at the same safety margin.
    H4.2.1   open         c=0.45 Removing lookahead from the airbench96-style base costs >=0.3 pp of mean accuracy at a fixed epoch count, equivalent to about 1 epoch, and raises the per-seed accuracy std.

Settings: frozen patch-whitening conv (2x2, fit in prepare on real train images), dirac init, widths 128/384/576, depth 3 per block, BatchNorm-bias lr x64, Nesterov SGD lr 9 / wd 0.012 / bs 1024, label smoothing 0.3, lookahead, alternating flip plus translate-2 on GPU. The whole train set lives on the GPU as uint8 and is loaded in prepare. Use channels_last with bf16/fp16 autocast. torch.compile and warmup run in build() on synthetic data, covering the full batch, the final partial batch and eval shapes. Train for 10 epochs. Eval is a plain forward with no TTA and must handle any B from 1 to 1024.  -> First feasible run. Accuracy 0.752-0.765 (point estimate ~0.758), time 9-14 s, against 59.3 s for the ResNet9 baseline. If accuracy is below 0.753, the next step is 11 epochs.
I003 p4 queued   H1.1.3   Third point of the epoch sweep on the base recipe: 9 epochs, or 11 if the 10-epoch run missed 0.753. Fit accuracy against epochs with the 8.5 and 10 points and find the knee at 0.753 to within 0.5 epochs.  -> Accuracy rises roughly linearly at about 0.4-0.6 pp per epoch. 9 epochs gives about 0.753-0.756: feasible with ~10% less time than 10 epochs, or a near-miss that pins the knee at about 9.3.
I004 p3 queued   H4.1.1   Rerun the feasible base recipe unchanged (identical commit config, fixed seeds 0-2) to measure the run-to-run noise floor from nondeterministic kernels and timing jitter.  -> Accuracy within 0.15 pp and time within 3% of the original run. This sets the inconclusive threshold for later comparisons and the safety margin needed above 0.753.
I005 p3 queued   H1.3.1   Base recipe at its knee epoch count, with label smoothing 0.2 instead of 0.3. Nothing else changes.  -> Accuracy drops ~0.3-0.5 pp and time is unchanged. Confirms LS 0.3 for CIFAR-100. If the drop is under 0.15 pp, mark it inconclusive.
I006 p2 queued   H4.2.1   Base recipe at its knee epoch count with lookahead removed: plain Nesterov SGD, no weight averaging. Same lr, wd and schedule.  -> Accuracy drops ~0.3-0.6 pp (worth about 1 epoch) and per-seed spread widens. Time falls slightly (<2%) from skipping the averaging step. Confirms lookahead is worth keeping.
I007 p2 queued   H1.2.1   Explore: on the base recipe, switch the 4D conv filters to Muon (Newton-Schulz orthogonalized momentum, lr ~0.24, momentum 0.6, nesterov). Biases, BatchNorm and the head stay on Nesterov SGD. Use batch size 2000 with linear decay to zero, and keep the epoch count at the SGD knee.  -> At equal epochs, accuracy is +0.3 to +0.8 pp, so 1-1.5 fewer epochs are needed and time is ~10-15% lower at the knee. Risk: Newton-Schulz overhead and a large-batch accuracy drop could cancel the gain.
I008 p2 queued   H2.3.1   Explore: on the feasible base, run the first ~35% of epochs on 24 px random crops and the rest at full 32 px. Compile both resolutions in build(). Same epoch count as the knee.  -> Time falls ~8-12%. Accuracy drops 0.2-0.5 pp. Net gain only if adding back ≤0.5 epoch recovers 0.753.
I009 p3 queued   H2.2.1   Built on the first feasible airbench96-style base (I001/I003 knee). Make one systems change and leave the recipe alone. Move the whole training step into one torch.compile'd function: forward, backward, Nesterov SGD update and lookahead blend. Apply the update with torch._foreach_* ops (or SGD foreach/fused=True) so there is no per-parameter Python loop. Pass lr and the lookahead schedule as 0-d GPU tensors so changing them never triggers a recompile. Compile and warm up this function in build() on synthetic data, covering the full batch and the final partial batch. Keep the epoch count, seeds, lr, wd, LS and widths identical to the base.  -> Time drops about 5-10% against the base at the same epoch count, because Python and kernel-launch overhead is a noticeable share of a run near 10 s. Accuracy stays within 0.2 pp of the base, so feasibility is unchanged. If the gain is under 3%, the step was not launch-bound and H2.2 loses support.

I003 p4 queued   H1.1.3   Third point of the epoch sweep on the base recipe: 9 epochs, or 11 if the 10-epoch run missed 0.753. I004 p3 queued   H4.1.1   Rerun the feasible base recipe unchanged (identical commit config, fixed seeds 0-2) to measure the run-to-run noise floor from nondeterministic kernels and timing jitter.  -> Accuracy within 0.15 pp and time within 3% of the original run. This sets the inconclusive threshold for later comparisons and the safety margin needed above 0.753.
I005 p3 queued   H1.3.1   Base recipe at its knee epoch count, with label smoothing 0.2 instead of 0.3. Nothing else changes.  -> Accuracy drops ~0.3-0.5 pp and time is unchanged. Confirms LS 0.3 for CIFAR-100. If the drop is under 0.15 pp, mark it inconclusive.
I006 p2 queued   H4.2.1   Base recipe at its knee epoch count with lookahead removed: plain Nesterov SGD, no weight averaging. Same lr, wd and schedule.  -> Accuracy drops ~0.3-0.6 pp (worth about 1 epoch) and per-seed spread widens. Time falls slightly (<2%) from skipping the averaging step. Confirms lookahead is worth keeping.
I007 p2 queued   H1.2.1   Explore: on the base recipe, switch the 4D conv filters to Muon (Newton-Schulz orthogonalized momentum, lr ~0.24, momentum 0.6, nesterov). Biases, BatchNorm and the head stay on Nesterov SGD. Use batch size 2000 with linear decay to zero, and keep the epoch count at the SGD knee.  -> At equal epochs, accuracy is +0.3 to +0.8 pp, so 1-1.5 fewer epochs are needed and time is ~10-15% lower at the knee. I008 p2 queued   H2.3.1   Explore: on the feasible base, run the first ~35% of epochs on 24 px random crops and the rest at full 32 px. Compile both resolutions in build(). Same epoch count as the knee.  -> Time falls ~8-12%. Accuracy drops 0.2-0.5 pp. Net gain only if adding back ≤0.5 epoch recovers 0.753.
I009 p3 queued   H2.2.1   Built on the first feasible airbench96-style base (I001/I003 knee). Make one systems change and leave the recipe alone. Move the whole training step into one torch.compile'd function: forward, backward, Nesterov SGD update and lookahead blend. H3       open         c=0.50 Fixed overheads in the timed prepare/train are >10% of a run of about 10 s. These include loading and decoding data on 4 CPUs, host-to-device copies, normalization, whitening fit, CPU augmentation, and compile or autotune that leaks into the timed region. They can be cut without changing the learning recipe, while staying within the rules.
  H3.1     open         c=0.60 Keep the whole training set on the GPU as a uint8/half tensor, loaded in prepare, and run augmentation (flip, translate/crop, cutout) as vectorized GPU ops. This removes the bottleneck of a 4-CPU dataloader.
    H3.1.1   open         c=0.50 With data and augmentation on the GPU, prepare (load, transfer, normalize, whitening fit) takes <=1.0 s, and per-epoch time is not CPU-bound: GPU utilization stays >=90% during train.
  H3.2     open         c=0.60 Every compile, autotune and warmup happens in build() on synthetic inputs, covering every shape used later (full and final partial train batch, eval batch sizes). That way nothing recompiles inside the timed region, and no real data is touched in build.
    H3.2.1   open         c=0.60 After warmup in build, the first epoch's time is within 10% of later epochs, and no recompilation happens during prepare or train. Eval of any batch size B=1..1024 finishes in <5 s.
H4       open         c=0.50 The variance across seeds and runs, measured against the 0.753 cutoff on 3 seeds, decides how much over-training is needed. Measuring the noise floor and reducing variance (lookahead/EMA) lets a recipe run closer to its knee, below 0.758 without being fragile.
  H4.1     open         c=0.55 With seeds fixed, repeated runs of the same recipe differ only through nondeterministic kernels and GPU timing jitter. Both are small compared with the effects we want to detect.
    H4.1.1   open         c=0.60 Rerunning an identical recipe 2-3 times gives a spread in mean accuracy of <=0.15 pp and a spread in mean time of <=3%. Smaller differences are marked inconclusive (~).
  H4.2     open         c=0.50 Weight averaging (lookahead or EMA) raises accuracy at low epoch counts and lowers the spread across seeds. This allows fewer epochs at the same safety margin.
    H4.2.1   open         c=0.45 Removing lookahead from the airbench96-style base costs >=0.3 pp of mean accuracy at a fixed epoch count, equivalent to about 1 epoch, and raises the per-seed accuracy std.

sealed E002 (blind)
# D001: E000 shows the template is only a stub (accuracy 0.012, time 0.11 s), so the first real experiment has to put a full recipe in place, and the exact settings are still unknown. The search should answer this: which published from-scratch recipe reaches ≥75.3% CIFAR-100 top-1 test accuracy without test-time augmentation in the fewest epochs or least wall-clock time on one GPU? What does its accuracy-vs-epochs curve look like near 75% (needed for H1.1.1, H1.1.2 and H1.1.3), and how much do TTA, label smoothing (H1.3), lookahead/EMA (H4.2) and width (H1.5) each contribute? Exact hyperparameters are needed: widths, lr, wd, batch size, LS, whitening and epochs.

Request R001 (auto, after E000); 80 papers found, 4 relevant, 4 read in full, 5 verified claims; cost $0.54

**Bottom line:** none of the verified cards answers the question. No card gives an airbench96-style recipe, CIFAR-100 accuracy without TTA near 75% for an approximately 10-epoch run, an accuracy-vs-epochs curve, or ablations for TTA, label smoothing (LS), lookahead or EMA, or width. The tree's exact settings (128/384/576 widths, depth 3, LS 0.3, lr 9, wd 0.012, batch size 1024, the ~0.65 pp TTA estimate) come only from its search sources, not from checked quotes. Treat them as unverified starting values.

**What the cards say, and their conditions**

- **C0001 (Super-Convergence), conditional on H1 and H1.1.** On ResNet-56 / CIFAR-100, a one-cycle large-learning-rate schedule beats step schedules in 25 epochs, compared with 100-400. This supports the H1 premise that schedule-driven sample efficiency dominates. But the regime is 25 epochs on ResNet-56, not about 10 epochs on an airbench-style net, so it says nothing about where the 0.753 knee falls. The tree also has no node for schedule shape (warmup fraction, peak lr, decay to zero). That is a gap worth one Lvl3 prediction once a base recipe exists.
- **C0002 (Super-Convergence), conditional on H1.2 and H1.2.1.** It used total batch size 512, with a small generalization gap at large batches. That is far from Muon at batch size 2000, so it neither supports nor refutes H1.2. Ignore it for now.
- **C0005 (Multilayer Lookahead), conditional on H4.2 and H1.1.1/H1.1.2.** Lookahead-style averaging reaches 70% on CIFAR-100 in 30 epochs (ResNet-18, batch size 50, before any lr decay). That is consistent with averaging speeding up early progress. But it is 5 pp below the bar, uses tiny batches, and has no averaging-off control, so it cannot size the H4.2.1 effect. Keep H4.2.1 as a planned ablation.
- **C0003 and C0004 (ResNet strikes back), not relevant.** They cover ImageNet ResNet-50 at around 300 epochs. Don't use them.

**Bearing on results:** E000 (0.012 accuracy, 0.11 s) is the stub template. None of the cards explains or contradicts it, and none contradicts a current belief.

**What to do next**

1. **E001:** put the H1.1 airbench96-style recipe in place exactly as the tree states it, with no TTA. Include GPU-resident data and augmentation (H3.1), and compile and warm up in `build` (H2.1, H3.2). Run it at about 12 epochs, deliberately above the 10-epoch claim, so the first run is likely to clear 0.753. The literature cannot place the knee, so overshoot once rather than miss.
2. **Find the curve yourselves.** Sweep 9, 10, 11 and 12 epochs to measure the accuracy-vs-epochs relationship (H1.1.1, H1.1.2, H1.1.3). Before trusting any difference under about 0.3 pp, rerun one recipe to get the noise floor (H4.1.1).
3. **Keep confidences as they are.** Confidence in H1.1.1, H1.1.2, H1.3.1, H1.5.1 and H4.2.1 should not change. Their sources were not verified, so each needs its own ablation run.
4. **Search again** with targeted queries before the ablations: "airbench CIFAR-100", "94% on CIFAR-10 in 3.29 seconds" (arXiv 2404.00498, for its TTA, whitening and lookahead ablations), and the hlb-CIFAR10 and airbench96 code for exact hyperparameters.

## Claims
- C0001 (conditional; H1, H1.1): Supports the H1 premise that a one-cycle large-lr schedule sharply cuts the epochs needed on CIFAR-100, but only shown for ResNet-56 at 25 epochs. It does not locate the ~10-epoch knee. The tree lacks a schedule-shape node; add one after the base recipe exists.
- C0002 (conditional; H1.2, H1.2.1): Batch size 512 with a small generalization gap; too far from Muon at batch size 2000 to inform H1.2. No action.
- C0005 (conditional; H4.2, H1.1.1, H1.1.2): Lookahead reaches 70% on CIFAR-100 in 30 epochs (ResNet-18, batch size 50), consistent with averaging speeding early progress. It is below the bar and has no ablation, so H4.2.1 still needs its own lookahead-off run.
- C0003 (untested; H1): ImageNet ResNet-50 long-schedule recipe; not relevant to a ~10-epoch CIFAR-100 speedrun. Ignore.
- C0004 (untested; H1): Offers timm baselines; no bearing on this task. Ignore.

## Sources
- C0001: Super-Convergence: Very Fast Training of Neural Networks Using Large Learning Rates (2017) https://arxiv.org/abs/1708.07120v3
- C0002: Super-Convergence: Very Fast Training of Neural Networks Using Large Learning Rates (2017) https://arxiv.org/abs/1708.07120v3
- C0003: ResNet strikes back: An improved training procedure in timm (2021) https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2110.00476
- C0004: ResNet strikes back: An improved training procedure in timm (2021) https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2110.00476
- C0005: Multilayer Lookahead: a Nested Version of Lookahead (2021) https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.14254v1

No card gives an airbench96-style recipe, CIFAR-100 accuracy without TTA near 75% for an approximately 10-epoch run, an accuracy-vs-epochs curve, or ablations for TTA, label smoothing (LS), lookahead or EMA, or width. The tree's exact settings (128/384/576 widths, depth 3, LS 0.3, lr 9, wd 0.012, batch size 1024, the ~0.65 pp TTA estimate) come only from its search sources, not from checked quotes. Treat them as unverified starting values.

**What the cards say, and their conditions**

- **C0001 (Super-Convergence), conditional on H1 and H1.1.** On ResNet-56 / CIFAR-100, a one-cycle large-learning-rate schedule beats step schedules in 25 epochs, compared with 100-400. This supports the H1 premise that schedule-driven sample efficiency dominates. But the regime is 25 epochs on ResNet-56, not about 10 epochs on an airbench-style net, so it says nothing about where the 0.753 knee falls. The tree also has no node for schedule shape (warmup fraction, peak lr, decay to zero). That is a gap worth one Lvl3 prediction once a base recipe exists.
- **C0002 (Super-Convergence), conditional on H1.2 and H1.2.1.** It used total batch size 512, with a small generalization gap at large batches. That is far from Muon at batch size 2000, so it neither supports nor refutes H1.2. Ignore it for now.
- **C0005 (Multilayer Lookahead), conditional on H4.2 and H1.1.1/H1.1.2.** Lookahead-style averaging reaches 70% on CIFAR-100 in 30 epochs (ResNet-18, batch size 50, before any lr decay). That is consistent with averaging speeding up early progress. But it is 5 pp below the bar, uses tiny batches, and has no averaging-off control, so it cannot size the H4.2.1 effect. Keep H4.2.1 as a planned ablation.
- **C0003 and C0004 (ResNet strikes back), not relevant.** They cover ImageNet ResNet-50 at around 300 epochs. Don't use them.

**Bearing on results:** E000 (0.012 accuracy, 0.11 s) is the stub template. None of the cards explains or contradicts it, and none contradicts a current belief.

**What to do next**

1. **E001:** put the H1.1 airbench96-style recipe in place exactly as the tree states it, with no TTA. Include GPU-resident data and augmentation (H3.1), and compile and warm up in `build` (H2.1, H3.2). Run it at about 12 epochs, deliberately above the 10-epoch claim, so the first run is likely to clear 0.753. The literature cannot place the knee, so overshoot once rather than miss.
2. **Find the curve yourselves.** Sweep 9, 10, 11 and 12 epochs to measure the accuracy-vs-epochs relationship (H1.1.1, H1.1.2, H1.1.3). Before trusting any difference under about 0.3 pp, rerun one recipe to get the noise floor (H4.1.1).
3. **Keep confidences as they are.** Confidence in H1.1.1, H1.1.2, H1.3.1, H1.5.1 and H4.2.1 should not change. Their sources were not verified, so each needs its own ablation run.
4. **Search again** with targeted queries before the ablations: "airbench CIFAR-100", "94% on CIFAR-10 in 3.29 seconds" (arXiv 2404.00498, for its TTA, whitening and lookahead ablations), and the hlb-CIFAR10 and airbench96 code for exact hyperparameters.

## Claims
- C0001 (conditional; H1, H1.1): Supports the H1 premise that a one-cycle large-lr schedule sharply cuts the epochs needed on CIFAR-100, but only shown for ResNet-56 at 25 epochs. It does not locate the ~10-epoch knee. The tree lacks a schedule-shape node; add one after the base recipe exists.
- C0002 (conditional; H1.2, H1.2.1): Batch size 512 with a small generalization gap; too far from Muon at batch size 2000 to inform H1.2. No action.
- C0005 (conditional; H4.2, H1.1.1, H1.1.2): Lookahead reaches 70% on CIFAR-100 in 30 epochs (ResNet-18, batch size 50), consistent with averaging speeding early progress. It is below the bar and has no ablation, so H4.2.1 still needs its own lookahead-off run.

- C0004 (untested; H1): Offers timm baselines; no bearing on this task. Ignore.

"""Diagnostic (not an experiment): where does a training step's time go?

Usage: CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=3 taskset -c 20-23 uv run python drafts/profile_step.py [submission_dir]
"""

import importlib.util
import sys
import time
from pathlib import Path

import torch

sys.path.insert(0, str(Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]))
from benchmark.api import BuildContext  # noqa: E402
from benchmark.data import load_split  # noqa: E402

sub = Path(sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "submissions/arena") / "submission.py"
spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location("sub", sub)
mod = importlib.util.module_from_spec(spec)
spec.loader.exec_module(mod)

torch.set_num_threads(4)
dev = torch.device("cuda")
data = load_split(Path("data"), train=True)
state = mod.build(BuildContext(dev, {"epochs": 2}))
torch.manual_seed(0)
mod.prepare(state, data, 0)
torch.cuda.synchronize()
t = time.perf_counter()
mod.train(state)
torch.cuda.synchronize()
print(f"2-epoch train: {time.perf_counter() - t:.3f}s")

# Pure GPU time of fwd+bwd+opt for one batch, vs wall time
x = state.padded[:1024, :, :32, :32].contiguous(memory_format=torch.channels_last)
y = state.labels[:1024]
opt = state.optimizer
for _ in range(5):
    mod.train_step(state, opt, x, y)
torch.cuda.synchronize()
n = 50
t = time.perf_counter()
for _ in range(n):
    mod.train_step(state, opt, x, y)
torch.cuda.synchronize()
print(f"train_step wall: {(time.perf_counter() - t) / n * 1e3:.2f} ms/step")

from torch.profiler import ProfilerActivity, profile  # noqa: E402

with profile(activities=[ProfilerActivity.CPU, ProfilerActivity.CUDA]) as prof:
    for _ in range(10):
        mod.train_step(state, opt, x, y)
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
print(prof.key_averages().table(sort_by="cuda_time_total", row_limit=25))

"""Diagnostic: cost of the per-epoch / per-5-step overheads in train()."""
import importlib.util, sys, time
from pathlib import Path
import torch
sys.path.insert(0, str(Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]))
from benchmark.api import BuildContext
from benchmark.data import load_split
sub = Path(sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "submissions/arena") / "submission.py"
spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location("sub", sub); mod = importlib.util.module_from_spec(spec); spec.loader.exec_module(mod)
torch.set_num_threads(4)
dev = torch.device("cuda")
data = load_split(Path("data"), train=True)
state = mod.build(BuildContext(dev, {"epochs": 2}))
torch.manual_seed(0)
def T(name, fn, n=10):
    fn(); torch.cuda.synchronize(); t = time.perf_counter()
    for _ in range(n): fn()
    torch.cuda.synchronize(); print(f"{name}: {(time.perf_counter()-t)/n*1e3:.2f} ms")
torch.cuda.synchronize(); t=time.perf_counter(); mod.prepare(state, data, 0); torch.cuda.synchronize(); print(f"prepare {time.perf_counter()-t:.3f}s")
T("augment", lambda: mod.augment(state.padded, state.flip_bits, 0, 2))
imgs = mod.augment(state.padded, state.flip_bits, 0, 2)
def permute():
    perm = torch.randperm(50000, device=dev); imgs[perm].contiguous(memory_format=torch.channels_last); state.labels[perm]
T("permute", permute)
T("lookahead", lambda: state.lookahead.update(state.model, 0.5), n=50)
EOF

"""Diagnostic: tight-loop step time over a sustained run vs a short burst, and per-epoch train() time."""
import importlib.util, sys, time
from pathlib import Path
import torch
sys.path.insert(0, str(Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]))
from benchmark.api import BuildContext
from benchmark.data import load_split
sub = Path(sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "submissions/arena") / "submission.py"
spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location("sub", sub); mod = importlib.util.module_from_spec(spec); spec.loader.exec_module(mod)
torch.set_num_threads(4)
dev = torch.device("cuda")
data = load_split(Path("data"), train=True)
state = mod.build(BuildContext(dev, {}))
torch.manual_seed(0)
mod.prepare(state, data, 0)
imgs = mod.augment(state.padded, state.flip_bits, 0, 2).contiguous(memory_format=torch.channels_last)
opt = state.optimizer
for block in range(8):
    torch.cuda.synchronize(); t = time.perf_counter()
    for i in range(48):
        mod.train_step(state, opt, imgs[i*1024:(i+1)*1024], state.labels[i*1024:(i+1)*1024])
    torch.cuda.synchronize(); print(f"block {block}: {(time.perf_counter()-t)/48*1e3:.2f} ms/step")
time.sleep(3)
torch.manual_seed(0); mod.prepare(state, data, 0); torch.cuda.synchronize()
t = time.perf_counter(); mod.train(state); torch.cuda.synchronize(); print(f"train(): {time.perf_counter()-t:.3f}s for {state.total_steps} steps")
EOF

# D002: E001 cleared the bar on its first try: 0.7584 at 10 epochs in 9.28 s. That leaves about 0.5 pp of slack, so the next gains have to come from fewer epochs at the same accuracy. The open lever with the most potential and the most uncertainty is H1.2 (confidence 0.5): replacing Nesterov SGD on the conv filters of a small CNN with Muon, with or without a larger batch. The search should answer two things. Does Muon (or a related orthogonalized or second-order-lite optimizer) cut the epochs and wall-clock time needed to reach a fixed accuracy for short-budget CNN training on CIFAR-scale data, by how much, and with which hyperparameters (lr, momentum, Newton-Schulz steps, batch size, which parameters get Muon)? And is the per-step overhead small enough to keep a net time gain in a run of about 10 s?

Request R002 (auto, after E001); 80 papers found, 2 relevant, 2 read in full, 10 verified claims; cost $0.50

## Lit digest: Muon for short-budget CNN training (H1.2)

**Short answer:** none of the verified cards measures Muon in a regime like ours: a small CNN on CIFAR, trained for about 10 epochs to a fixed accuracy, scored on wall-clock time. So the literature neither supports nor refutes H1.2.1's ≥10% time gain. airbench94_muon, the source for H1.2, has no verified card here. The cards only show that Muon is plausible for convolutions and suggest how to keep its per-step cost low.

**Where the loop stands.** The 9-epoch recipe scores 0.7552 in 8.34 s (E002). The 10-epoch recipe scores 0.7584 in 9.28 s (E001). That is about 0.32 pp per epoch, below the ≥0.4 pp H1.1.3 predicted. Each epoch costs about 0.94 s. E003 reproduced E002's accuracy exactly, with about a 1% difference in time. So accuracy is deterministic given the seeds, and differences of 0.1 pp are real. To be worth it, Muon has to save at least about 1 epoch at matched accuracy, net of its Newton–Schulz (NS) cost.

**Muon on conv kernels (all conditional).**
- **C0006, C0007, C0008:** Muon-C beats both unfolded Muon and Adam. Early FID is 9.87 vs 22.26 vs 51.31. It needs 36–38% fewer FLOPs to reach final quality, and still wins under equal tuning budgets.
  - All of this is CIFAR-10 *flow matching* over 40k–400k steps, a long-horizon generative task. It does not transfer to a 9-epoch classifier.
- **C0009:** the same result on ImageNet-32, also flow matching. It is mapped to H1.3, but it really bears on H1.2.
- **C0010:** Muon-C gives the best validation accuracy for ResNet/ConvNeXt classification on ImageNet-100. The card gives no effect size and no time-to-target. It is also mapped to H1.3 by mistake.
- **Untested mechanism:** Muon-C's "operator-aligned" treatment of conv kernels is a different way to reshape the kernel than airbench's plain flattening. The tree has no node for it. Add it as an H1.2 child only if plain Muon (H1.2.1) shows a signal first.

**Keeping NS overhead down (relevant to the per-step question).**
- **C0012:** a cubic NS schedule uses 10 matmuls instead of 15 for quintic, a third less optimizer compute. This is untested here and bears on H1.2.1's net time.
- **C0013, C0014, C0015:** final quality barely depends on how exactly NS orthogonalizes. Cubic5 matches quintic within about 1e-3 loss, but the evidence is from GPT-2 and 1–4B MoE/Mamba models (conditional). Implication: use few NS steps (3–5) in bf16, and batch NS across the conv layers.

**Recommended action.** Run H1.2.1 directly as an experiment, because the literature can't settle it:
- Muon on the 4D conv filters only.
- Nesterov SGD for the BatchNorm biases, the whitening layer (frozen anyway) and the head.
- Muon lr ~0.24, momentum 0.6, 3–5 NS steps.
- Compare at **9 and 8 epochs** against E002. Try batch size 1024 first, then 2000.
- Use the deterministic baseline (E003) to treat ≥0.1 pp as real.
- Profile the optimizer step separately. If NS takes more than about 5% of step time, try cubic NS (C0012) before dropping H1.2.

Leave the confidence in H1.2 at 0.5. These cards give no evidence for updating it.

## Claims
- C0006 (conditional; H1.2): Muon-C beats unfolded Muon and Adam early in training, but only in long-horizon CIFAR-10 flow matching. It does not transfer to a 9-epoch classifier; test H1.2.1 directly.
- C0007 (conditional; H1.2, H1.2.1): Muon-C reaches the target with 36-38% fewer FLOPs in a generative 400k-step regime. Treat this as a weak prior that Muon can save compute; it says nothing about time-to-0.753 in ~9 epochs.
- C0008 (conditional; H1.2): Muon-C still wins under equal tuning budgets, but the FID gap is small and the task is different. Do not update H1.2 confidence.
- C0009 (conditional; H1.2): Wrongly mapped to H1.3; it is about the optimizer, not label smoothing. The task is ImageNet-32 flow matching, a regime this loop does not use.
- C0010 (untested; H1.2): Muon-C beats the baselines on ImageNet-100 CNN classification, but with no effect size or time-to-target. Operator-aligned kernel reshaping is a mechanism the tree lacks; add it as an H1.2 child only if plain Muon shows a signal.
- C0011 (conditional; H1.2): General motivation for Muon (approximately orthogonal updates) with no measured effect size. Gives no help in sizing the epoch saving.
- C0012 (untested; H1.2.1): Cubic NS needs 10 matmuls instead of 15, a third less optimizer compute. Use it if profiling shows NS costs more than about 5% of step time in the ~8 s run.
- C0013 (conditional; H1.2): How exactly NS orthogonalizes barely affects final loss (GPT-2). This justifies using few NS steps in bf16 for the CNN, but confirm accuracy at 9 epochs.
- C0014 (conditional; H1.2.1): Cubic5 matches quintic NS within about 1e-3 loss on 1-4B models. Weak support for the cheaper schedule in our small CNN.
- C0015 (conditional; H1.2.1): Cubic5 matches training quality at lower overhead in LM settings. Treat it as the fallback if Muon's step cost erases its epoch saving.

## Sources
- C0006: Muon-C: Operator-Aligned Muon for Convolutional Kernels (2026) https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.09676v1
- C0007: Muon-C: Operator-Aligned Muon for Convolutional Kernels (2026) https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.09676v1
- C0008: Muon-C: Operator-Aligned Muon for Convolutional Kernels (2026) https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.09676v1
- C0009: Muon-C: Operator-Aligned Muon for Convolutional Kernels (2026) https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.09676v1
- C0010: Muon-C: Operator-Aligned Muon for Convolutional Kernels (2026) https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.09676v1
- C0011: How Much Orthogonalization Does Muon Need? (2026) https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2606.00371
- C0012: How Much Orthogonalization Does Muon Need? (2026) https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2606.00371
- C0013: How Much Orthogonalization Does Muon Need? (2026) https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2606.00371
- C0014: How Much Orthogonalization Does Muon Need? (2026) https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2606.00371
- C0015: How Much Orthogonalization Does Muon Need? (2026) https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2606.00371

class Lookahead:
    def __init__(self, model):
        self.ema = {k: v.detach().clone() for k, v in model.state_dict().items() if v.is_floating_point()}

    @torch.no_grad()
    def update(self, model, decay):
        for k, v in model.state_dict().items():
            if k in self.ema:
                self.ema[k].lerp_(v, 1 - decay)
                v.copy_(self.ema[k])


def make_optimizer(model, hyp, total_steps):
    bs = hyp["batch_size"]
    momentum = hyp["momentum"]
    kilostep_scale = 1024 * (1 + 1 / (1 - momentum))
    lr = hyp["lr"] / kilostep_scale
    wd = hyp["weight_decay"] * bs / kilostep_scale
    lr_biases = lr * hyp["bias_scaler"]
    whiten_bias = [model.whiten.bias]
    norm_biases = [p for k, p in model.named_parameters() if "norm" in k and p.requires_grad]
    other = [
        p
        for k, p in model.named_parameters()
        if "norm" not in k and p.requires_grad and p is not model.whiten.bias
    ]
    groups = [
        dict(params=whiten_bias, lr=lr_biases, weight_decay=wd / lr_biases),
        dict(params=norm_biases, lr=lr_biases, weight_decay=wd / lr_biases),
        dict(params=other, lr=lr, weight_decay=wd / lr),
    ]
    optimizer = torch.optim.SGD(groups, momentum=momentum, nesterov=True)
    for g in optimizer.param_groups:
        g["base_lr"] = g["lr"]
    return optimizer


def lr_factor(step, total_steps):
    warmup = int(total_steps * 0.23)
    if step < warmup:
        frac = step / warmup
        return 0.2 * (1 - frac) + 1.0 * frac
    frac = (step - warmup) / max(1, total_steps - warmup)
    return 1.0 * (1 - frac) + 0.07 * frac


def build(context: BuildContext):
    hyp = {**HYP, **context.parameters}
    device = context.device
    torch.backends.cudnn.benchmark = True
    torch.backends.cuda.matmul.allow_tf32 = True
    torch.backends.cudnn.allow_tf32 = True
    model = Net(context.num_classes, hyp["widths"], hyp["depth"], hyp["bn_momentum"], hyp["scale"])
    model = model.to(device).to(memory_format=torch.channels_last)
    step_model = torch.compile(model) if hyp["compile"] and device.type == "cuda" else model
    state = SimpleNamespace(model=model, step_model=step_model, context=context, hyp=hyp)
    # Warm up compilation and cuDNN autotuning on synthetic data (state is reset in prepare).
    bs = hyp["batch_size"]
    x = torch.rand(bs, 3, 32, 32, device=device).to(memory_format=torch.channels_last)
    y = torch.randint(0, context.num_classes, (bs,), device=device)
    model.train()
    opt = make_optimizer(model, hyp, 10)
    for _ in range(3):
        train_step(state, opt, x, y)
    if device.type == "cuda":
        torch.cuda.synchronize()
    return state


def train_step(state, optimizer, x, y):
    with torch.autocast(state.context.device.type, dtype=torch.bfloat16):
        logits = state.step_model(x)
        loss = F.cross_entropy(logits.float(), y, label_smoothing=state.hyp["label_smoothing"], reduction="sum")
    optimizer.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
    loss.backward()
    optimizer.step()


def prepare(state, data: TrainingData, seed: int) -> None:
    hyp = state.hyp
    device = state.context.device
    model = state.model
    for m in model.modules():
        if m is not model and hasattr(m, "reset_parameters"):
            m.reset_parameters()
        if isinstance(m, nn.BatchNorm2d):
            m.reset_running_stats()
    images = data.images.to(device, non_blocking=True).float().div_(255)
    labels = data.labels.to(device, non_blocking=True)
    mean = images.mean(dim=(0, 2, 3), keepdim=True)
    std = images.std(dim=(0, 2, 3), keepdim=True)
    with torch.no_grad():
        model.mean.copy_(mean)
        model.std.copy_(std)
        init_whitening(model.whiten, ((images[:5000] - mean) / std))
    r = hyp["translate"]
    state.padded = F.pad(images, (r, r, r, r), mode="reflect") if r > 0 else images
    state.labels = labels
    state.flip_bits = torch.rand(len(images), device=device) < 0.5
    steps_per_epoch = len(images) // hyp["batch_size"]
    state.total_steps = int(steps_per_epoch * hyp["epochs"])
    state.optimizer = make_optimizer(model, hyp, state.total_steps)
    state.lookahead = Lookahead(model) if hyp["lookahead"] else None
    model.train()


def train(state) -> nn.Module:
    hyp = state.hyp
    model = state.model
    optimizer = state.optimizer
    total = state.total_steps
    bs = hyp["batch_size"]
    n = len(state.labels)
    r = hyp["translate"]
    alpha = ((0.95**5) * (torch.arange(total + 1) / total) ** 3).tolist()
    step = 0
    epoch = 0
    while step < total:
        whiten_on = epoch < hyp["whiten_bias_epochs"]
        imgs = augment(state.padded, state.flip_bits, epoch, r) if r > 0 else state.padded
        perm = torch.randperm(n, device=imgs.device)
        imgs = imgs[perm].contiguous(memory_format=torch.channels_last)
        labels = state.labels[perm]
        for i in range(n // bs):
            if step >= total:
                break
            f = lr_factor(step, total)
            for gi, g in enumerate(optimizer.param_groups):
                g["lr"] = g["base_lr"] * f if (gi != 0 or whiten_on) else 0.0
            train_step(state, optimizer, imgs[i * bs : (i + 1) * bs], labels[i * bs : (i + 1) * bs])
            step += 1
            if state.lookahead is not None and step % 5 == 0:
                state.lookahead.update(model, decay=alpha[step])
        epoch += 1
    if state.lookahead is not None:
        state.lookahead.update(model, decay=1.0)
    model.eval()
    return model

def _sgd_update(params, grads, bufs, lr, wd: float, momentum: float):
    # Nesterov SGD with torch.optim.SGD semantics (zero-initialised buffers give the same first step).
    with torch.no_grad():
        torch._foreach_add_(grads, params, alpha=wd)
        torch._foreach_mul_(bufs, momentum)
        torch._foreach_add_(bufs, grads)
        torch._foreach_add_(grads, bufs, alpha=momentum)
        torch._foreach_mul_(grads, lr)
        torch._foreach_sub_(params, grads)


@torch.compile
def _lookahead_update(ema, current, weight):
    with torch.no_grad():
        diffs = torch._foreach_sub(current, ema)
        torch._foreach_mul_(diffs, weight)
        torch._foreach_add_(ema, diffs)
        torch._foreach_copy_(current, ema)


class FusedSGD:
    """Nesterov SGD whose per-group lr is a 0-d GPU tensor, updated by one compiled foreach kernel per group."""

    def __init__(self, groups, momentum, device):
        self.groups = groups
        self.momentum = momentum
        for g in groups:
            g["bufs"] = [torch.zeros_like(p) for p in g["params"]]
            g["lr_t"] = torch.zeros((), device=device)

    def reset(self):
        for g in self.groups:
            torch._foreach_zero_(g["bufs"])

    def set_lr(self, factors):
        for g, f in zip(self.groups, factors):
            g["lr_t"].fill_(g["base_lr"] * f)

    def zero_grad(self):
        for g in self.groups:
            for p in g["params"]:
                p.grad = None

    def step(self):
        for g in self.groups:
            _sgd_update(g["params"], [p.grad for p in g["params"]], g["bufs"], g["lr_t"], g["wd"], self.momentum)


class Lookahead:
    def __init__(self, model, device):
        self.current = [v for v in model.state_dict().values() if v.is_floating_point()]
        self.ema = [v.detach().clone() for v in self.current]
        self.weight = torch.zeros((), device=device)

    def reset(self):
        torch._foreach_copy_(self.ema, self.current)

    def update(self, decay):
        self.weight.fill_(1 - decay)
        _lookahead_update(self.ema, self.current, self.weight)


def make_optimizer(model, hyp, device):
    bs = hyp["batch_size"]
    momentum = hyp["momentum"]
    kilostep_scale = 1024 * (1 + 1 / (1 - momentum))
    lr = hyp["lr"] / kilostep_scale
    wd = hyp["weight_decay"] * bs / kilostep_scale

"""Apply I012 (Muon on 4D conv filters except the frozen whitening conv) to submissions/arena/submission.py."""
p = "submissions/arena/submission.py"
s = open(p).read()

s = s.replace('''    "compile": True,
}''', '''    "compile": True,
    "muon_lr": 0.24,
    "muon_momentum": 0.6,
    "ns_steps": 5,
}''')

muon = '''
@torch.compile
def zeropower_via_newtonschulz5(G, steps: int, eps: float = 1e-7):
    a, b, c = (3.4445, -4.7750, 2.0315)
    X = G.bfloat16()
    X = X / (X.norm() + eps)
    transposed = G.size(0) > G.size(1)
    if transposed:
        X = X.T
    for _ in range(steps):
        A = X @ X.T
        B = b * A + c * A @ A
        X = a * X + B @ X
    if transposed:
        X = X.T
    return X


class Muon(torch.optim.Optimizer):
    """Orthogonalized Nesterov momentum for conv filters, with per-step weight-norm projection (airbench94_muon)."""

    def __init__(self, params, lr, momentum, ns_steps):
        super().__init__(params, dict(lr=lr, momentum=momentum, ns_steps=ns_steps))

    @torch.no_grad()
    def step(self):
        for group in self.param_groups:
            for p in group["params"]:
                g = p.grad
                state = self.state[p]
                if "momentum_buffer" not in state:
                    state["momentum_buffer"] = torch.zeros_like(g)
                buf = state["momentum_buffer"]
                buf.mul_(group["momentum"]).add_(g)
                g = g.add(buf, alpha=group["momentum"])
                p.mul_(len(p) ** 0.5 / p.norm())
                g2 = g.reshape(len(g), -1)
                scale = max(1.0, g2.size(0) / g2.size(1)) ** 0.5
                update = zeropower_via_newtonschulz5(g2, group["ns_steps"]).view(g.shape)
                p.add_(update, alpha=-group["lr"] * scale)


'''
s = s.replace("class Lookahead:", muon + "class Lookahead:")

s = s.replace('''    other = [
        p
        for k, p in model.named_parameters()
        if "norm" not in k and p.requires_grad and p is not model.whiten.bias
    ]
    groups = [
        dict(params=whiten_bias, lr=lr_biases, weight_decay=wd / lr_biases),
        dict(params=norm_biases, lr=lr_biases, weight_decay=wd / lr_biases),
        dict(params=other, lr=lr, weight_decay=wd / lr),
    ]
    optimizer = torch.optim.SGD(groups, momentum=momentum, nesterov=True)
    for g in optimizer.param_groups:
        g["base_lr"] = g["lr"]
    return optimizer''', '''    filters = [p for k, p in model.named_parameters() if p.ndim == 4 and p.requires_grad]
    other = [
        p
        for k, p in model.named_parameters()
        if "norm" not in k and p.requires_grad and p is not model.whiten.bias and p.ndim != 4
    ]
    groups = [
        dict(params=whiten_bias, lr=lr_biases, weight_decay=wd / lr_biases),
        dict(params=norm_biases, lr=lr_biases, weight_decay=wd / lr_biases),
        dict(params=other, lr=lr, weight_decay=wd / lr),
    ]
    sgd = torch.optim.SGD(groups, momentum=momentum, nesterov=True)
    muon = Muon(filters, lr=hyp["muon_lr"], momentum=hyp["muon_momentum"], ns_steps=hyp["ns_steps"])
    for opt in (sgd, muon):
        for g in opt.param_groups:
            g["base_lr"] = g["lr"]
    return [sgd, muon]''')

s = s.replace('''    optimizer.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
    loss.backward()
    optimizer.step()''', '''    for opt in optimizer:
        opt.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
    loss.backward()
    for opt in optimizer:
        opt.step()''')

s = s.replace('''            for gi, g in enumerate(optimizer.param_groups):
                g["lr"] = g["base_lr"] * f if (gi != 0 or whiten_on) else 0.0''', '''            for gi, g in enumerate(optimizer[0].param_groups):
                g["lr"] = g["base_lr"] * f if (gi != 0 or whiten_on) else 0.0
            for g in optimizer[1].param_groups:
                g["lr"] = g["base_lr"] * f''')
open(p, "w").write(s)
EOF

  optimizer-list plumbing; fix and relaunch.
EOF

# D003: The base recipe is now at its knee: 9 epochs, about 8.34 s, accuracy 0.7552-0.7560. Label smoothing turned out not to matter (E004 refutes H1.3.1). Systems tuning has a ceiling, so the next big drop in time has to come from needing fewer epochs. The most decision-relevant open branch is H1.2/H1.2.1, at confidence 0.4-0.5. Does an orthogonalized-momentum optimizer (Muon, or relatives such as Shampoo/SOAP/PSGD with Newton-Schulz orthogonalization) on the conv filters of a small ResNet/airbench-style CNN cut the epochs needed to reach a fixed accuracy, compared with tuned Nesterov SGD? Does that hold in a very short (<10 epoch) CIFAR regime, ideally CIFAR-100? If so, what settings are reported: lr, momentum, Newton-Schulz steps, batch size, which parameters go to Muon versus SGD, and schedule? And does the per-step overhead of orthogonalization eat into the wall-clock gain?

Request R003 (auto, after E004); 80 papers found, 4 relevant, 4 read in full, 13 verified claims; cost $0.61

## Muon on conv filters in a short CIFAR run: what the cards show

**Short answer: the cards don't settle it.** None of them compares Muon with tuned Nesterov SGD on CIFAR classification in under 10 epochs, on CIFAR-10 or CIFAR-100. None reports lr, momentum, Newton-Schulz (NS) step count or batch size for a small CNN. The settings in H1.2.1 (lr ~0.24, momentum 0.6, Nesterov, bs ~2000, linear decay) still come only from the `airbench94_muon.py` source. **H1.2 stays at about 0.45–0.5. Nothing here supports or refutes it.**

**What the cards do give:**
- **Conv kernels, other tasks (conditional).** These results are generative or long-horizon, and the baselines are other Muon variants or Adam, not tuned SGD:
  - **C0016:** on CIFAR-10 flow matching at 40k iterations, FID was 9.87 for Muon-C vs 22.26 for flattened ("unfolded") Muon vs 51.31 for Adam.
  - **C0018:** the same pattern on ImageNet-32.
  - **C0019:** Muon-C gave the best ImageNet-100 accuracy on ResNet-34/50 and ConvNeXtV2-T.
  - None of this transfers directly to a 9-epoch, 0.753 knee.
- **A mechanism the tree lacks (untested).**
  - **C0016/C0017:** how you split a 4D conv kernel into matrices before orthogonalizing matters. Splitting by frequency (Muon-C) beat both the flattened version and splitting by spatial offset (Muon-S). It also had the stronger *early* trajectory, which is the part that counts in a 9-epoch run.
  - airbench94_muon flattens kernels. If plain Muon fails, try a frequency-wise variant before closing H1.2.
- **NS quality depends on each matrix (untested).**
  - **C0024, C0026, C0027:** finite-step NS quality depends on each matrix's stable rank and condition number. A single fixed step count under- or over-orthogonalizes some layers.
  - Here the shapes differ a lot: the frozen whitening layer, which must stay excluded, the 128-wide stem and the 576×5184 last block.
  - If Muon underperforms, first check NS steps per layer (about 3 vs 5), then the lr.
- **Overhead (conditional, LLM only).**
  - **C0020/C0021:** Newton-Muon used 6% fewer steps to the target loss but saved only about 4% of wall-clock time. Extra optimizer math eats roughly a third of the step saving there.
  - Expect the same here. Muon must save clearly more than 10% of steps to meet H1.2.1's ≥10% time target.
- **Not relevant to this question:** C0022 (theory only), C0023 (no effect size), C0025/C0028 (Muon in LLM pretraining).

**How this bears on the loop's results:**
- **E005** refuted H2.2.1: the fused, fully compiled step cut 0.001 s and lost 0.1 pp. When adding Muon, leave the existing SGD path for BatchNorm biases (lr ×64) and the head untouched.
- Put only the 3×3 conv filters on Muon, in a separately compiled NS function warmed up in build().

**Next step:** run H1.2.1 directly.
1. Use the airbench94_muon settings at 9 epochs, comparing bs 2000 against the current bs 1024, and log the share of step time spent in NS.
2. Then test 8 epochs. The E002–E006 spread suggests the knee moves about 0.4 pp per epoch.

# D004: The best feasible recipe is the airbench96-style net at 9 epochs: 0.7542–0.7552 accuracy in about 8.26 s. That margin over 0.753 is very thin. The systems changes failed (E005 and E007 refuted H2.2.1 and H2.1), and dropping to 8.5 epochs missed the bar (E006). The lever that remains is sample efficiency per epoch. Lookahead alone was worth about 1.1 pp (E008), which shows that optimizer and averaging dynamics matter a great deal in this regime. The question: in very short CIFAR training (about 5–10 epochs, small ResNet/airbench-style CNNs), does Muon or another orthogonalized optimizer reach a given accuracy in fewer epochs or less wall-clock time than tuned Nesterov SGD with lookahead? Specifically:
- which hyperparameters work (lr, momentum, Newton-Schulz steps, batch size, which parameters get Muon);
- whether it combines with lookahead or EMA weight averaging;
- how large the gain is on CIFAR-100 compared with CIFAR-10.
This directly tests H1.2 / H1.2.1 (confidence 0.40–0.50, untested). The answer decides whether the next experiments port airbench94_muon's optimizer or stay with SGD and tune averaging or the schedule.

Request R004 (auto, after E008); 80 papers found, 0 relevant, 0 read in full, 0 verified claims; cost $0.47

## Digest: Muon vs. SGD+lookahead in short CIFAR training

**No verified literature evidence was found.** No claim card survived quote-checking, so this digest cites none. Nothing here confirms or rules out a Muon advantage on CIFAR-100 at 5–10 epochs. That includes the hyperparameters (lr, momentum, Newton-Schulz steps, batch size, which parameters get Muon), whether it combines with lookahead or EMA, and the size of any gain on CIFAR-100 versus CIFAR-10. The airbench94_muon reference in H1.2 is still an unverified source pointer, and its CIFAR-10 numbers should not be carried over to CIFAR-100.

### What the loop's own results imply

- **Correction to the question:** the current best is E010, not E007: **0.7551 accuracy at 8.09 s**. The amax-pool change (supports H2.2) took about 0.17 s off E007. Systems work is not fully exhausted, but each change gains only about 2%.
- **Noise floor:** E003 reproduced E002's accuracy exactly (0.75523). On the 3 fixed seeds, accuracy is effectively deterministic, so even a 0.1 pp difference in a single run is real *for these seeds*. The 40-seed official judgment still adds sampling risk that 3 seeds cannot measure. A margin of about 0.2 pp, as at E010, is thin.
- **Optimizer dynamics matter:** removing lookahead cost 1.1 pp (E008, supports H4.2.1). That is about 2 epochs' worth, given that 8.5 → 9 epochs moved accuracy by about 0.4 pp (E006 vs E002). An optimizer change has room to beat schedule tuning, but this is a prior, not evidence about Muon.

### Recommendation

With no literature, H1.2.1 has to be settled by direct experiment, and the test should be cheap and unconfounded:

1. **Port Muon for 4D conv filters only.** Flatten each filter to (out, in·k·k). Keep Nesterov SGD for BatchNorm biases, the whitening layer (frozen), and the head. **Keep lookahead and the 9-epoch schedule unchanged**, and leave batch size at 1024. Moving to bs 2000 at the same time would make any result impossible to attribute. Use the airbench94_muon-style defaults in H1.2.1 (lr ~0.24, momentum 0.6, Nesterov, 5 NS steps) as an unverified starting point. Compare against E010 at matched epochs: accuracy is the primary readout, and time shows the NS overhead.
2. **If accuracy rises ≥0.4 pp at 9 epochs**, test 8 epochs next; that is where a time win would show up. **If it falls**, try one lr ×2 / ×0.5 pair and drop lookahead only as a separate arm. Lookahead's averaging may overlap with Muon's update normalization, but that is untested here and in the literature found.
3. **If Muon fails**, stay with SGD. The best-supported lever left is averaging (EMA on top of lookahead, H4.2), because E008 shows that is where the large effects are.

Treat H1.2 / H1.2.1 as **untested, with confidence unchanged**. No literature update applies.

## Claims
- none

## Sources
- none

I018 (running): Exploit E014. Port the E014 Muon optimizer exactly as it was onto the tip E010 commit (5aa9aa5: LS 0.2, cudnn.benchmark, max-autotune-no-cudagraphs, F.max_pool2d head). Muon settings: conv filters except 
the frozen whitening conv, Nesterov momentum 0.6, lr 0.24, 5 quintic NS steps in bf16, update scaled by sqrt(max(1,out/in)) on the flattened [out,in*k*k] matrix. BN biases and the head stay on the existing SGD, and looka
head is kept. Make ONE recipe change: epochs 9 -> 8, with the lr, Muon and lookahead schedules scaled to the new step count. The final partial batch shape is compiled in build(). Before launching, run the one-step finite
-gradient check (drafts/debug_nan.py), because the compiled NS and Muon graph is new to the tip's compile mode. Log the optimizer step time separately.
expected: New best. Accuracy 0.756-0.764 (point ~0.760): E014's +1.3 pp at 9 epochs minus ~0.8-1.2 pp for one fewer epoch. Time 7.75-8.10 s (point ~7.95 s): tip per-epoch ~0.89 s plus ~0.09 s/epoch Muon overhead measured
 in E014, times 8 epochs. Below 0.753 would mean Muon's gain collapses at shorter horizons; then retry at 8.5 epochs.
  H1.2.1 open c=0.35: Muon (lr ~0.24, momentum 0.6, Nesterov, 3 NS steps, flattened filters) on the conv filters only, with lookahead, bs 1024 and the 9-epoch schedule kept, gives >=+0.3 pp mean accuracy over the tip at 
9 epochs. That is enough to reach >=0.753 in >=10% less time (<=7.3 s) at its own knee.
  H1.2 open c=0.45: Using Muon (orthogonalized momentum, 3-5 Newton-Schulz steps) on the 4D conv filters, and Nesterov SGD for BN biases, the whitening bias and the head, cuts the epochs and wall-clock time needed on CIF
AR-100. Lookahead must be kept, because on CIFAR-100 it is worth ~1 pp (E008), whereas airbench94_muon drops it.
  H1 open c=0.60: The score is mainly set by how many epochs it takes to reach mean accuracy >=0.753 on seeds 0-2. Recipe changes that improve sample efficiency (weight averaging and the lr tail, optimizer, lr/wd, width)
 can move the knee below 8 epochs (<=7.3 s) and are worth more than systems work. Measured effect sizes so far: lookahead ~1 pp, LS 0.2 vs 0.3 ~0, one epoch ~0.3-0.8 pp near the knee.

"""Diagnostic: wall time of Muon.step and SGD.step alone, for NS steps 5 and 3."""
import importlib.util, sys, time
from pathlib import Path
import torch
sys.path.insert(0, str(Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]))
from benchmark.api import BuildContext
spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location("sub", "submissions/arena/submission.py"); mod = importlib.util.module_from_spec(spec); spec.loader.exec_module(mod)
dev = torch.device("cuda")
state = mod.build(BuildContext(dev, {}))
x = torch.rand(1024, 3, 32, 32, device=dev).to(memory_format=torch.channels_last); y = torch.randint(0, 100, (1024,), device=dev)
opts = mod.make_optimizer(state.model, state.hyp, 100)
mod.train_step(state, opts, x, y)
def T(name, fn, n=50):
    for _ in range(3): fn()
    torch.cuda.synchronize(); t = time.perf_counter()
    for _ in range(n): fn()
    torch.cuda.synchronize(); print(f"{name}: {(time.perf_counter()-t)/n*1e3:.3f} ms")
T("full train_step", lambda: mod.train_step(state, opts, x, y))
T("sgd.step", opts[0].step)
for ns in (5, 3):
    opts[1].param_groups[0]["ns_steps"] = ns
    T(f"muon.step ns={ns}", opts[1].step)
EOF

"""Diagnostic: CPU wall vs GPU time of Muon.step (ns from argv) inside the real train step."""
import importlib.util, sys, time
from pathlib import Path
import torch
from torch.profiler import ProfilerActivity, profile
sys.path.insert(0, str(Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]))
from benchmark.api import BuildContext
spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location("sub", "submissions/arena/submission.py"); mod = importlib.util.module_from_spec(spec); spec.loader.exec_module(mod)
ns = int(sys.argv[1]) if len(sys.argv) > 1 else 5
dev = torch.device("cuda")
state = mod.build(BuildContext(dev, {"ns_steps": ns}))
x = torch.rand(1024, 3, 32, 32, device=dev).to(memory_format=torch.channels_last); y = torch.randint(0, 100, (1024,), device=dev)
opts = mod.make_optimizer(state.model, state.hyp, 100)
for _ in range(5): mod.train_step(state, opts, x, y)
torch.cuda.synchronize(); t = time.perf_counter()
for _ in range(50): mod.train_step(state, opts, x, y)
torch.cuda.synchronize(); print(f"ns={ns} full train_step wall: {(time.perf_counter()-t)/50*1e3:.3f} ms")
with profile(activities=[ProfilerActivity.CUDA]) as prof:
    for _ in range(10): opts[1].step()
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
gpu = sum(e.self_device_time_total for e in prof.key_averages()) / 10 / 1e3
print(f"ns={ns} muon.step GPU time: {gpu:.3f} ms")
EOF
for ns in 5 3; do CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=3 taskset -c 20-23 uv run python drafts/time_muon.py $ns 2>&1 | grep "^ns="; done

"""Draft: replace the per-parameter Muon loop with one compiled update over all conv filters.

Same math as Muon.step (Nesterov momentum, weight-norm projection, NS quintic, sqrt(max(1,out/in)) scale);
lr is a 0-d GPU tensor so schedule changes never recompile.
"""
p = "submissions/arena/submission.py"
s = open(p).read()
def rep(a, b):
    global s
    assert a in s, a
    s = s.replace(a, b)
rep('''class Muon(torch.optim.Optimizer):
    """Orthogonalized Nesterov momentum for conv filters, with per-step weight-norm projection (airbench94_muon)."""

    def __init__(self, params, lr, momentum, ns_steps):
        super().__init__(params, dict(lr=lr, momentum=momentum, ns_steps=ns_steps))

    @torch.no_grad()
    def step(self):
        for group in self.param_groups:
            for p in group["params"]:
                g = p.grad
                state = self.state[p]
                if "momentum_buffer" not in state:
                    state["momentum_buffer"] = torch.zeros_like(g)
                buf = state["momentum_buffer"]
                buf.mul_(group["momentum"]).add_(g)
                g = g.add(buf, alpha=group["momentum"])
                p.mul_(len(p) ** 0.5 / p.norm())
                g2 = g.reshape(len(g), -1)
                scale = max(1.0, g2.size(0) / g2.size(1)) ** 0.5
                update = zeropower_via_newtonschulz5(g2, group["ns_steps"]).view(g.shape)
                p.add_(update, alpha=-group["lr"] * scale)
''', '''def _newtonschulz(G, steps: int, eps: float = 1e-7):
    a, b, c = (3.4445, -4.7750, 2.0315)
    X = G.bfloat16()
    X = X / (X.norm() + eps)
    transposed = G.size(0) > G.size(1)
    if transposed:
        X = X.T
    for _ in range(steps):
        A = X @ X.T
        B = b * A + c * A @ A
        X = a * X + B @ X
    if transposed:
        X = X.T
    return X


@torch.compile(dynamic=False)
def _muon_update(params, grads, bufs, lr, momentum: float, ns_steps: int):
    with torch.no_grad():
        torch._foreach_mul_(bufs, momentum)
        torch._foreach_add_(bufs, grads)
        updates = torch._foreach_add(grads, bufs, alpha=momentum)
        for p, g in zip(params, updates):
            p.mul_(len(p) ** 0.5 / p.norm())
            g2 = g.reshape(len(g), -1)
            scale = max(1.0, g2.size(0) / g2.size(1)) ** 0.5
            u = _newtonschulz(g2, ns_steps).view(g.shape)
            p.sub_(u.float() * (lr * scale))


class Muon:
    """Orthogonalized Nesterov momentum for conv filters, with per-step weight-norm projection (airbench94_muon).

    One compiled graph updates all filters; lr is a 0-d GPU tensor.
    """

    def __init__(self, params, lr, momentum, ns_steps):
        self.params = list(params)
        self.bufs = [torch.zeros_like(p) for p in self.params]
        self.lr_t = torch.tensor(float(lr), device=self.params[0].device)
        self.param_groups = [dict(lr=lr)]
        self.momentum = momentum
        self.ns_steps = ns_steps

    def zero_grad(self, set_to_none=True):
        for p in self.params:
            p.grad = None

    def step(self):
        self.lr_t.fill_(self.param_groups[0]["lr"])
        _muon_update(self.params, [p.grad for p in self.params], self.bufs, self.lr_t, self.momentum, self.ns_steps)
''')
open(p, "w").write(s)

IFNSO: Iteration-Free Newton–Schulz Orthogonalization Chen Hu huch67@mail2.sysu.edu.cn Qianxi Zhao zhaoqx9@mail2.sysu.edu.cn Xiaochen Yuan xcyuan@mpu.edu.mo Hong Zhang dmrzhang@buaa.edu.cn Ding Yuan dyuan@buaa.edu.cn Yanbin Wu wuyb53@mail2.sysu.edu.cn Xiying Li stslxy@mail.sysu.edu.cn organization=School of Intelligent Systems Engineering, addressline=Sun Yat-sen University, city=Shenzhen, postcode=518107, state=Guangdong, country=PR China organization=Faculty of Applied Sciences, addressline=Macao Polytechnic University, city=Macao, postcode=999078, state=Macao, country=PR China organization=School of Astronautics, addressline=Beihang University, city=Beijing, postcode=100191, state=Beijing, country=PR China Abstract The Newton–Schulz (NS) iteration has become a key technique for orthogonalization in optimizers such as Muon and for optimization on the Stiefel manifold. Despite its effectiveness, the conventional NS iteration incurs significant computational overhead due to repeated high-dimensional matrix multiplications. To overcome these limitations, we propose Iteration-Free Newton–Schulz Orthogonalization (IFNSO), a novel framework that replaces the traditional iterative structure with a unified and Iteration-Free structure with learnable coefficients. In order to optimize these coefficients stably, we introduce a new polynomial which is constrained to 1 as the input approaches 1. Additionally, we employ an exponential term selection strategy, an analysis of the contribution of each term, to further improve performance. Extensive experiments demonstrate that IFNSO achieves superior performance compared to existing methods. # D005: E014 was surprising. Muon on the conv filters, with lookahead kept, reached 0.768 at 9 epochs, +1.3 pp over the tip and far above the predicted range. But the run took 9.18 s against the tip's 8.09 s, so the optimizer step costs about 13% more time. That much accuracy headroom is worth roughly 2 epochs, which makes H1.2 the most decision-relevant open branch. The question: how can Muon's per-step cost be cut, and how should its hyperparameters be retuned so that a Muon recipe clears 0.753 at about 6.5-7.5 epochs in less time than the tip? Specifically: (a) cheaper orthogonalization, via fewer Newton-Schulz steps (3 vs 5), tuned quintic coefficients, batching or stacking same-shape filters into one batched matmul, lower precision, or orthogonalizing less often than every step; (b) how Muon's lr, momentum, Nesterov use, and the warmup/decay schedule should change when the run is shortened to fewer epochs or steps; (c) whether Muon interacts with lookahead or EMA weight averaging, and with batch size, in short training runs.

Request R005 (auto, after E014); 80 papers found, 11 relevant, 5 read in full, 25 verified claims; cost $0.83

## Muon cost and retuning: what the literature says

**Where things stand.** The loop has already answered part of the question. Moving from 5 to 3 Newton-Schulz (NS) steps (E017) kept accuracy and saved about 0.23 s at 8 epochs. That puts the cost of the 3 remaining steps at roughly 0.3 s, about 4% of the new tip (E018: 7.39 s, 0.7596). E018 also clears the gate with about 0.65 pp to spare at 7.5 epochs, and one epoch is worth about 0.3–0.8 pp. **Cutting epochs (7.0, then 6.5) is still worth more than any change to orthogonalization**, which can save at most about 4%.

**(a) Cheaper orthogonalization**
- **C0047** (explains): standard Muon uses 5 NS steps. E017 shows 3 is enough here, as in airbench94_muon.
- **C0036, C0039, C0040, C0041** (conditional; tested on NanoGPT and synthetic matrices): tuned Chebyshev-type (CANS) coefficients reach the same orthogonalization quality with fewer matmuls. A larger polynomial derivative at zero also helps convergence. Next: try **2 steps with CANS-style coefficients** against the 3-step tip. Expect at most about 1.5% time saved. That is near the jitter, so it needs a paired rerun.
- **C0031, C0034** (untested mechanism): batching same-shape matrices across layers into one batched matmul (bmm) leaves the optimizer state and dynamics unchanged. Here each block has two convs of the same shape: 128×1152, 384×3456 and 576×5184. Stacking each pair is math-identical apart from re-draw noise (H4.1). Measure the optimizer step time per step first. H2.2 found little launch overhead, so the gain may be small.
- **C0029, C0030, C0033, C0032** (conditional; transformer setting): tiled NS trades spectral coupling for cost, with a "full early, tiled late" schedule. This is a plausible way to orthogonalize less in late steps, but there is no evidence for convs or short runs.
- **C0051** (explains): bf16 is adequate for this spectral computation, consistent with E014's bf16 NS working.
- **C0050, C0052, C0053** (conditional; LLM-scale): adaptive spectral bounds cut 2–3 NS steps for a target error. The machinery is too heavy for a 7 s run and low priority.
- **C0042–C0046** (IFNSO): evidence is weak (MNIST, batch size 32). Skip.

**(b) lr, momentum and schedule under fewer steps.** No card addresses this. E019 already refuted raising the Muon lr to 0.36 (−1 pp). The pre-registered follow-up is 0.16–0.20, and Muon momentum (0.6) is still untuned.

**(c) Interaction with lookahead/EMA and batch size.** No card addresses short-run averaging. **C0049** (untested here) is theory showing Muon can fail to converge for nearly all mini-batch sizes on simple problems. It does not bear on 7-epoch runs, so leave batch size at 1024.

**Recommended next steps, in order:**
1. 7.0 epochs on E018.
2. Muon lr 0.18.
3. Batch the same-shape NS pairs.
4. 2-step CANS coefficients.

## Claims
- C0047 (explains; H1.2.1): Standard Muon uses 5 NS steps. E017 shows 3 is enough here; the remaining NS cost is ~4% of time.
- C0036 (conditional; H1.2.1): CANS coefficients beat standard NS at the same matmul count (NanoGPT). Try 2 tuned steps against 3.

content.thinking: Implementing stacked same-shape filter pairs so Newton-Schulz runs as a single `bmm` per shape group within one compiled step, then I'll verify it matches current Muon numerically before timing it.

cp submissions/arena/submission.py /tmp/old_submission.py && python - <<'EOF'
p = "submissions/arena/submission.py"
s = open(p).read()
start = s.index("@torch.compile(dynamic=False)\ndef zeropower_via_newtonschulz5")
end = s.index("class Lookahead:")
new = '''def _newtonschulz(G, steps: int, eps: float = 1e-7):
    """Quintic Newton-Schulz on a stack of matrices G [k, m, n], in bf16."""
    a, b, c = (3.4445, -4.7750, 2.0315)
    X = G.bfloat16()
    X = X / (X.norm(dim=(1, 2), keepdim=True) + eps)
    transposed = G.size(1) > G.size(2)
    if transposed:
        X = X.mT
    for _ in range(steps):
        A = X @ X.mT
        B = b * A + c * A @ A
        X = a * X + B @ X
    if transposed:
        X = X.mT
    return X


@torch.compile(dynamic=False)
def _muon_update(params, grads, bufs, lr, momentum: float, ns_steps: int, shape_groups: tuple):
    with torch.no_grad():
        torch._foreach_mul_(bufs, momentum)
        torch._foreach_add_(bufs, grads)
        updates = torch._foreach_add(grads, bufs, alpha=momentum)
        for idx in shape_groups:
            G = torch.stack([updates[i].reshape(len(updates[i]), -1) for i in idx])
            scale = max(1.0, G.size(1) / G.size(2)) ** 0.5
            U = _newtonschulz(G, ns_steps)
            for j, i in enumerate(idx):
                p = params[i]
                p.mul_(len(p) ** 0.5 / p.norm())
                p.sub_(U[j].view(p.shape).float() * (lr * scale))


class Muon:
    """Orthogonalized Nesterov momentum for conv filters, with per-step weight-norm projection (airbench94_muon).

    One compiled graph updates all filters; same-shape filters are orthogonalized together as one batched matmul,
    and the lr is a 0-d GPU tensor so schedule changes never recompile.
    """

    def __init__(self, params, lr, momentum, ns_steps):
        self.params = list(params)
        self.bufs = [torch.zeros_like(p) for p in self.params]
        self.lr_t = torch.tensor(float(lr), device=self.params[0].device)

Hua Huang † † thanks: huah@nvidia.com Affiliation: NVIDIA Abstract Muon optimizers improve neural-network training by replacing ill-conditioned momentum updates with approximately semi-orthogonal updates. This motivates a practical question: how much orthogonalization does Muon actually require? We study this question using a relaxed cubic Newton–Schulz schedule derived directly for Muon’s low precision singular value band. The resulting five-step cubic construction uses ten dominant matrix multiplications, compared with fifteen for five quintic Newton–Schulz iterations. The cubic schedule is not intended as a more accurate polar solver; instead, it is a principled low-cost variant that lets us probe the relation between polar accuracy, spectral shaping, and training quality. Across synthetic diagnostics, NanoGPT ablations, and training experiments on hybrid MoE/Mamba models, we find that training quality is not governed monotonically by polar-decomposition accuracy: truncated Polar Express, Muon-Jordan, cubic Newton–Schulz, and an explicit FP32 SVD polar factor can reach nearly indistinguishable final loss on GPT-2 Small, and cubic5 matches the Muon-Jordan quintic update within about validation loss on hybrid MoE/Mamba models with one billion to four billion parameters. These results support cubic5 as a practical low-cost Muon orthogonalization variant, with empirical evidence of training-quality parity in the settings tested. 1 Introduction 1.1 The Muon Optimizer Muon is a newly proposed optimizer for matrix-valued hidden layer parameters in neural networks [ 9 ] . It can be viewed as stochastic gradient descent with momentum followed by an orthogonalization step. Let be a weight matrix, its stochastic gradient, and a momentum buffer. A simplified Muon update is (1) (2) If is a singular value decomposition, then (3) Thus exact Muon would preserve the singular vectors of the momentum update but replace all nonzero singular values by one. Jordan et al. motivate this operation empirically by observing that transformer momentum updates are often nearly low-rank: a few directions dominate the update, while many “rare” directions have small singular values but may still matter for learning [ 9 ] . Orthogonalization can therefore be understood as a spectral reshaping operation that amplifies these suppressed directions. This perspective is different from the standard numerical linear algebra objective of computing a highly accurate polar factor. In neural network training, the update must remain useful after interaction with momentum, learning rate schedules, normalization, weight decay, stochastic gradients, and low precision arithmetic. An exact SVD polar factor is the natural mathematical reference point, but it need not optimize training loss. The central question of this work is therefore not merely whether a Newton–Schulz iteration converges to the polar factor, but how accurately Muon must orthogonalize its updates to preserve training quality. The key observation behind these iterations is that odd matrix polynomials act diagonally on singular values. If and (4) then (5) The matrix problem can therefore be studied through scalar polynomial maps on the singular values. Classical polar decomposition [ 6 , 5 , 2 , 11 , 7 , 13 , 12 ] algorithms and recently proposed hybrid polar decomposition method [ 8 ] optimize these polynomials for high accuracy convergence to one. Muon, however, is used in a deep learning regime where low precision approximate directions can be sufficient. This creates room for polynomial schedules that are less accurate as polar solvers but cheaper or differently biased as spectral transforms. 1.2 Polynomial Polar Decompositions for Muon The original Muon implementation uses five iterations of a fixed quintic Newton–Schulz polynomial, (6) run in bfloat16 after Frobenius normalization [ 9 ] . We refer to this baseline as Muon-Jordan. Its coefficients were chosen for the relaxed Muon objective: after repeated composition, singular values are allowed to lie in a band around one rather than converging to machine precision. Liu et al. [ 10 ] further demonstrated that Muon can be scaled to larger Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models containing 16 billion parameters. Polar Express revisits this polynomial-design problem from the perspective of matrix sign and polar decomposition methods [ 1 ] . It uses an adaptive sequence of quintic polynomials chosen by a minimax criterion. This improves the quality of the polar approximation and, when inserted into Muon, can improve validation loss across learning rate sweeps. Polar Express keeps the same basic computational structure as standard quintic Newton–Schulz: each iteration applies a degree-five odd polynomial using three dominant matrix multiplications. A complementary direction is to reduce the cost of the same polynomial iteration by restructuring the computation. Gram Newton–Schulz observes that many Muon matrices are rectangular and that standard Newton–Schulz repeatedly forms symmetric Gram matrices [ 15 ] . By moving more work to the smaller Gram matrix and using hardware-aware symmetric kernels, Gram Newton–Schulz reduces the runtime of the orthogonalization step while preserving the underlying polynomial iteration. This is orthogonal to coefficient design: one can improve the polynomial, the kernel, or both. 1.3 Contributions This work uses a relaxed cubic construction to probe a broader question: how much orthogonalization does Muon need, and what kind of spectral shaping matters for training? We make the following contributions. • We derive an adaptive cubic Newton–Schulz schedule whose coefficients are chosen from the current worst-case lower singular value bound and a relaxed target band . • We identify a practical five-step schedule using the bfloat16 effective lower bound . This schedule uses 10 dominant matrix multiplications, compared with 15 for five quintic iterations. • We compare cubic5, truncated Polar Express, truncated Muon-Jordan, and an explicit FP32 SVD polar factor inside NanoGPT training. This separates polar-decomposition accuracy from optimizer quality: exact SVD does not improve over the strongest approximate Newton–Schulz updates in our GPT-2 Small runs. • We characterize a cost-quality frontier. Cubic5 is close to Polar Express and SVD at the default GPT-2 Small setting, and it remains within approximately validation loss of the Muon-Jordan quintic update on hybrid MoE/Mamba models with 1B to 4B parameters. These results support cubic5 as a viable low-cost Muon orthogonalization variant in the evaluated regimes, not as a uniformly better update rule. • We validate the scalar construction on synthetic matrices and show by microbenchmarking that reducing the polynomial degree lowers the cost of the orthogonalization subroutine. Our claims are intentionally calibrated. Cubic5 is not presented as a more accurate polar decomposition algorithm than Polar Express, nor as a uniformly better Muon update.
